title: There is something almost unbearable about the scene.
paragraphs: There is something almost unbearable about the scene.
A king is sitting comfortably in his winter palace.
Outside, the cold has settled over Jerusalem. Inside, a fire burns before him.
Then someone begins reading the Word of God.
Not a motivational speech.
Not flattering counsel.
Not words designed to protect the king’s feelings.
A warning.
A call to turn back.
A message of coming judgment—but also, hidden inside that warning, an astonishing doorway to mercy.
And the king does something that should make every generation uncomfortable.
He reaches for a knife.
Jeremiah 36 records one of the most disturbing confrontations with the Word of God in Scripture. King Jehoiakim does not merely disagree with the prophetic scroll. He does not simply ignore it.
As the scroll is being read, he cuts it apart.
Piece by piece.
Then he throws the pieces into the fire.
One after another.
Until the scroll is gone.
Or so he thinks.
Because Jehoiakim is about to discover something every rebellious human heart eventually discovers:
You can burn the page.
You cannot burn the God who spoke.
And perhaps that is why this ancient story feels frighteningly modern.
Because most of us will never sit on a throne in Jerusalem.
Most of us will never hold Jeremiah’s scroll in our hands.
Most of us will never take a literal knife to a manuscript of Scripture.
But there are quieter ways of cutting away the words of God.
A verse confronts the relationship we know is sinful…
Cut.
Jesus tells us to forgive…
Cut.
Scripture exposes our pride…
Cut.
God calls us to repent…
Cut.
The Bible confronts our sexual sin, greed, bitterness, dishonesty, hatred, self-righteousness, secret addiction, hypocrisy, or unbelief…
Cut.
We keep the verses that comfort us.
We remove the ones that confront us.

And eventually, without ever lighting a physical fire, we can construct a Christianity where Jesus comforts us but never commands us, forgives us but never transforms us, saves us from consequences but never becomes Lord of our lives.
That is why Jehoiakim’s burning scroll is not merely a strange episode about an ancient king.
It is a mirror.
And mirrors can hurt.
The story begins during the reign of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, as Babylon’s power is rising and Judah is moving toward catastrophe.
God tells Jeremiah:
“Take thee a roll of a book, and write therein all the words that I have spoken unto thee against Israel, and against Judah, and against all the nations…”
Then comes something crucial.
God explains why the warning is being written.
“ It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the evil which I purpose to do unto them; that they may return every man from his evil way; that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin.”
Jeremiah 36:2–3.
Read that again slowly.
Judgment is being announced.
But forgiveness is still being offered.
This is where people sometimes misunderstand biblical prophecy.
God’s warning is not evidence that He delights in destruction.
The warning itself is mercy.
The Hebrew language makes the invitation painfully clear.
The text speaks of the possibility that each person might “return” from his evil way.
The Hebrew verb is שׁוּב — shuv.
To turn.
To return.
To come back.
It is one of the great words of repentance in the Old Testament.
God is essentially saying:
Perhaps they will hear.
Perhaps they will turn.
Perhaps they will come home.
And then:
“I may forgive their iniquity and their sin.”
The Hebrew verb behind “forgive” is סָלַח — salach.
This is not the vocabulary of a God eager to crush repentant people.
This is the vocabulary of mercy being extended before judgment falls.
That changes the entire emotional atmosphere of Jeremiah 36.
The scroll Jehoiakim eventually burns is not merely a scroll of condemnation.
He is burning a warning that contains an invitation to forgiveness.
Think about that.
God could have remained silent.
Instead, He spoke.
God could have allowed Judah to continue blindly toward disaster.
Instead, He warned them.
God could have said, “You have gone too far.”
Instead, He left the door of repentance open.
That is grace before the fire.
Jeremiah dictates the words to Baruch son of Neriah, who writes them onto a scroll.
Because Jeremiah is restricted from going to the temple, Baruch takes the scroll and publicly reads the words of the LORD.
Eventually, the message reaches the officials.
They listen.
And unlike Jehoiakim, they are frightened.
Jeremiah 36:16 says:
“Now it came to pass, when they had heard all the words, they were afraid both one and other…”
They understood that these were not ordinary words.
Something was happening.
Something demanded a response.
Eventually the scroll is brought before King Jehoiakim.
And now the camera of Scripture seems to move into the king’s chamber.
Jeremiah 36:22 tells us:
“Now the king sat in the winterhouse in the ninth month: and there was a fire on the hearth burning before him.”
You can almost feel the contrast.
Outside: winter.
Inside: warmth.
The king is comfortable.
The Word of God is uncomfortable.
Jehudi begins reading the scroll.
Three or four columns are read.
Then the king reaches for what many English translations describe as a penknife or scribe’s knife.
He cuts the scroll.
And throws it into the fire.
Then another section is read.
Cut.
Fire.
More words.
Cut.
Fire.
Again.
And again.
Jeremiah 36:23 describes the horrifying rhythm:
“And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire…”
Imagine watching it happen.
Words Jeremiah had spoken.
Words Baruch had carefully written.
Words warning a nation.
Words calling sinners back.
Curling.
Blackening.
Becoming ash.
But perhaps the most chilling verse is the next one.
“Yet they were not afraid, nor rent their garments…”
Jeremiah 36:24.
No trembling.
No brokenness.
No repentance.
No torn garments.
The officials who first heard the scroll had been afraid.
The king hears the same warning and burns it.
Same Word.
Different heart.
And that should trouble us.
Because proximity to Scripture does not guarantee submission to Scripture.
A person can hear sermons for decades and still resist Christ.
A person can know Bible verses and still protect secret sin.
A person can own ten Bibles and surrender to none of them.
The question is not merely:
“Have I heard God’s Word?”
The deeper question is:
“What happens inside me when God’s Word contradicts me?”
That is where Jehoiakim becomes uncomfortably personal.
When Scripture confronts you, which one gets edited?
Your life?
Or the Bible?
Because there are only so many ways to respond when God says something we do not want to hear.
We can humble ourselves.
We can repent.
We can obey.
Or we can reach for the knife.
Sometimes our knife is sophisticated.
“That verse belonged to another culture.”
Sometimes it sounds compassionate.
“Surely God would never expect me to give this up.”
Sometimes it sounds theological.
“My God would never judge anyone.”
Sometimes it sounds wounded.
“You don’t know what they did to me, so I don’t have to forgive.”
Sometimes it sounds modern.
“Jesus understands. This is just who I am.”
And sometimes the knife is simply silence.
We stop reading the passages that disturb us.
We stop attending churches that challenge us.
We unfollow anyone who tells us what we do not want to hear.
We search until we find someone who will baptize what God told us to bury.
Cut.
Cut.
Cut.
Until we have created a Bible that never disagrees with us.
And then we call it faith.
But there is another detail in Jeremiah 36 that changes everything.
Jehoiakim burns the scroll.
And God tells Jeremiah to write it again.
“Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll…”
Jeremiah 36:28.
Jehoiakim destroyed the manuscript.
He did not destroy the message.
Then Jeremiah 36:32 tells us that another scroll was written containing the former words, and “there were added besides unto them many like words.”
The king’s knife did not silence God.
His fire did not erase God.
His throne did not intimidate God.
Jehoiakim could determine what happened to the parchment in his hands.
He could not determine what happened to the Word proceeding from the mouth of the LORD.
And history has supplied the irony.
Jehoiakim wanted the words gone.
Yet thousands of years later, we are reading about him because the Word he tried to destroy preserved the account of what he did.
The king died.
The fire died.
The palace disappeared.
The empire that threatened Judah eventually disappeared.
But the testimony remains.
“The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.”
Isaiah 40:8.
Yet if we stop there, we miss the greatest movement of the biblical story.
Because Jeremiah’s scroll points beyond itself.
Humanity’s deepest problem was never merely that we needed another written warning.
We needed rescue.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed a Savior.
And centuries after Jehoiakim sat beside his fire, the eternal Word entered our world.
John opens his Gospel with breathtaking language:
Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ Λόγος
En archē ēn ho Logos.
“In the beginning was the Word.”
And then:
καὶ ὁ Λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
kai ho Logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word was made flesh.”
The message of God did not remain ink on parchment.
The Word became flesh.
Jesus Christ entered human history.
And humanity did something even more horrifying than Jehoiakim did to Jeremiah’s scroll.
We rejected Him.
Mocked Him.
Stripped Him.
Beat Him.
Pressed thorns onto His head.
Drove nails through His hands and feet.
And lifted Him onto a Roman cross.
Jehoiakim tried to destroy God’s written warning.
At Calvary, sinful humanity tried to destroy the incarnate Word.
But again…
God had the final word.
The scroll came back.
And the Son rose from the dead.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus was not merely another prophet calling sinners home.
He is the Savior who made the way home possible.
At the cross, Christ bore sin.
Not metaphorically.
Not sentimentally.
Scripture says:
“Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree…”
1 Peter 2:24.
Paul writes:
2 Corinthians 5:21.
And the resurrection declares that death did not defeat Him.
The grave could no more silence Jesus than Jehoiakim’s fire could silence God’s Word.
So now the story turns toward you.
Not toward Jehoiakim.
Not toward Jeremiah.
Toward you.
What have you been cutting out?
What has Jesus been confronting that you keep pushing away?
What secret have you been defending?
What bitterness have you renamed “boundaries” because forgiveness feels too costly?
What compromise have you called freedom?
What conviction have you repeatedly silenced?
What would happen if, instead of cutting the Word, you finally allowed the Word to cut you?
Hebrews 4:12 says:
“For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword…”
The Word cuts.
But there is a difference between the knife in Jehoiakim’s hand and the sword in God’s hand.
Jehoiakim cut the Word because he wanted to preserve his rebellion.
God’s Word cuts us because God intends to expose what is killing us.
A surgeon cuts differently than an executioner.
God exposes not merely to humiliate, but to call sinners into the light.
He names sin because sin destroys.
He commands repentance because repentance leads us away from destruction.
He confronts because He loves.
And at the center of Christianity stands not a God shouting instructions from a safe distance, but Jesus Christ bearing our judgment Himself.
Maybe you have spent years cutting pages out of your heart.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you still attend church.
Maybe you still post verses.
Maybe your family thinks you are strong.
Maybe people ask you for prayer while you secretly wonder whether your own prayers still reach heaven.
Maybe your browser history tells one story and your Sunday face tells another.
Maybe you have become skilled at looking spiritually alive while privately starving.
Maybe you have failed again.
And again.
And again.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not to pretend your sin is smaller.
And the answer is not to believe your sin is bigger than Christ.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Return.
שׁוּב.
Shuv.
Come home.
The Gospel is not God pretending your rebellion never happened.
The Gospel is God dealing with your rebellion at the cross.
Grace does not say sin does not matter.
Grace says sin mattered so much that Jesus Christ shed His blood to redeem sinners from it.
And this is why our words at Gospel Warrior keep returning to the same theme:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not because He edits our past until evil becomes good.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance becomes unnecessary.
Jesus rewrites everything because the sinner who deserved judgment can become the forgiven child of God.
The ashamed can be cleansed.
The rebellious can surrender.
The prodigal can return.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
The person who spent years running from God can turn around and discover that Christ still calls sinners to Himself.
Jehoiakim held a knife.
You do not have to.
Put it down.
Stop negotiating with the verses that expose you.
Stop trying to create a Jesus who agrees with everything you already believe.
Let the real Jesus be Lord.
And if something inside you is saying, “I have gone too far,” remember what Jeremiah 36 itself revealed.
Before judgment came, God sent a message so that people might turn and be forgiven.
And the Gospel announces something greater still:
Christ has come.
Christ has died.
Christ has risen.
And forgiveness is proclaimed in His name.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn the moment into empty engagement.
Make the response mean something.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
But if biblical truth has helped you, supporting Gospel-centered work can help that work continue reaching people.
But the deeper reason to stay connected is not the merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is having truth in front of you when compromise begins whispering.
It is being reminded of Christ when shame tells you to hide.
It is being sharpened by Scripture when the world tells you to dull its edges.
Use them.
Share them.
Put biblical truth into the hands of someone who needs it.
And never confuse supporting ministry with purchasing God’s approval. If you share, share because someone may need the truth. If you give, give freely.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Christ already paid the price sinners could never pay.
A king.
A knife.
A scroll.
A fire.
Jehoiakim watches the pieces disappear into the flames and perhaps believes the troublesome voice has finally been silenced.
But he is wrong.
God speaks again.
Another scroll is written.
The message survives the king who tried to destroy it.
And centuries later, the Word becomes flesh.
Men reject Him too.
They pierce His hands.
They crucify Him.
They seal His body inside a tomb.
And for one dark Sabbath, perhaps hell itself could have imagined that the story was over.
Then Sunday came.
The stone moved.
The tomb opened.
Jesus Christ rose.
So remember this when your sin tells you the story is finished.
Remember it when shame tells you God could never use you.
Remember it when your past screams louder than your prayers.
Remember it when you are tempted to cut away whatever Scripture says because obedience feels painful.
The fire does not get the final word.
Your failure does not get the final word.
Your shame does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
Death itself does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
And maybe the page you have been trying hardest to cut from your life is the very page where Christ is waiting to begin writing grace.
